parties:
Fazlul Huq Chowdhury  ------- Petitioner.
Vs
Govt. of Bangladesh  ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J.—This rule under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh alls in question an order dated 22.7.77 (Annexure-C) of Respondent No.1, Government of Bangladesh, communicated under the signature of respondent 3, Joint Secretary, Establishment Division, compulsorily retiring the petitioner, a Circle Officer (Revenue) from service under rule 3(3)(b) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976. 2. Facts of the case, so far necessary for disposal of this rule, are that the petitioner entered the service of Government in 1951 as an Assistant Manager of Government Acquired Estates and, by efficient discharge of his duties, as he alleged, he was promoted as Circle Officer of Revenue in 1967. On 27th July, 1976 a departmental proceeding was started against him under the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1960 on an allegation that he had disobeyed the order of his superiors to send a "parawise statement with regard to the plaint" of a civil case, Misc. Case No.104 of 1975 which was pending against the Government in the Third Court of Munsif, Comilla, and that in consequence of this disobedience the said suit was decreed. He submitted his explanation denying the allegation and also appeared before the Enquiry Officer who held an enquiry into the matter. The Enquiry Officer however submitted a report to the Government holding him guilty. The report was accepted and the petitioner was compulsorily retired. The proceeding though started under the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1960, was concluded under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976 which repealed the former during the pendency of the proceedings. Being aggrieved by the impugned order the petitioner sent a notice demanding justice from respondent No.1 but did not get any reply whereupon he moved this-Court and obtained the rule. 

 3. Mr. Sirajul Hoq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has assailed the impugned order mainly on the ground that the petitioner, being a person in the service of the Republic, is protected under Article 135 of the Constitution of Bangladesh but the mandatory provision of this Article was not complied with in his case in that he was not given any opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment. In other words, no second show cause notice was given to him after the Enquiry officer submitted his report of the enquiry nor any copy thereof was given to him. 

 4. Mr. Quazi Shafiuddin Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing to support the impugned order has contended that reasonable opportunity was given Jo the petitioner to defend himself when the allegation in writing was forwarded to him and that a second opportunity to show cause is required neither under Article 135 of the Constitution nor under the Rules of 1976. Further, he has contended that the provision as to show cause notice is applicable only in the case of dismissal, removal or 'reduction in rank' and not in the case of compulsory retirement' and that compulsory retirement is not removal or dismissal from service and as such Article 135 of the Constitution cannot be invoked by the petitioner. Mr. Shafiuddin has lastly contended that the petitioner's application under Article 102 of the Constitution is not maintainable since an alternative remedy by way of review before the President of Bangladesh was available to the petitioner under the Rules of 1976. 

 5. There is no dispute that the enquiry which was started against petitioner under the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1960 was rightly concluded under the Rules of 1976 which contain specific provision to this effect. The rules of 1976, unlike the rules of 1960, do not provide for any second show cause notice. But Mr. Sirajul Huq's contention is that Article 135 of the Constitution provides for a second show case notice and this constitutional provision shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Service Rules since the petitioner is a person in the service of the republic. There is no dispute that the petitioner is a person in the service of the republic and is entitled to the protection of Constitution. Article 134(2) of the Constitution which is relevant to this case is quoted below:- 

 Mr. Shafiuddin has referred to the record of the proceedings and submitted that a "reasonable" opportunity to show cause as referred to in this Article, was given to the petitioner when he was given a charge sheet containing some allegations brought against him, and that this Article does not require such an opportunity to show cause second time. Mr. Sirajul Huq has contended that when an allegation is brought against a person no definite opinion is formed by the authorities as to his guilt and that a definite opinion is formed when the authorities arrive at a provisional finding of guilt on the conclusion of the enquiry and that before that stage is reached no 'action is proposed to be taken". In support of this contention he has relied upon a number of decisions, particularly, a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of The-High Commissioner for India and another Vs. I. M. Lall, A.I.R., 1948 P.C., 121. In that case a member of the Indian Civil Service, I. M. Lal, was removed from service on a proved charge of nepotism.' He challenged the order of removal by a suit alleging that after the enquiry officer submitted his report of the enquiry he was not given any opportunity to show cause against the punishment proposed to be awarded him as required under Section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. This section is quoted below:- 

 Contention of the government in that case was that section 240(3) did not require any second show cause notice but required only one notice which was actually given to the accused officer. Their Lordships of the Privy Council rejected the Government's contention and held that that a second show cause notice was mandatory and the first show cause notice served along with the Charge sheet referred to mere statement of allegations which, if proved, might result in the punishment suggested Relevent part of their Lordship's Judgment is quoted below :- 

 6. Mr. Shafiuddin has, however, fried to raise a new contention on this point stating that the Language of Article 135(2) of the Constitution of Bangladesh is not exactly the same as the language of section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. He has pointed out that in Article 135(2) the words "action proposed to be taken" are not there; but the words "that action" have been used. Mr. Sirajul Huq has submitted that the words "that action" necessarily mean the words "action proposed". In support of this view he has referred to the Bengali Text of the Constitution in which the words have been used. We do not think that there is any conflict between' the English Text and the Bengal Text on these words and are of the view that "that action" in this Article means "action proposed" to be taken. Even if there is any conflict between the two texts, in view of Article 153, it is the Bengali Text which shall prevail., In an enquiry as contemplated in Article 135(2) of the Constitution a proposed action means an action which has been proposed to be taken on the basis of a provisional finding of guilt arrived at and prior to that stage, the proposed action is mere hypothetical. In this connection an office Memorandum No.R.VI/S-37/77-80 dated 8th August, 1977 of the Government of Bangladesh has been placed before us by the, learned Assistant Attorney General. This relates to the Rules of 1976 as already referred to. It has been stated there that though Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules of 1976 do not provide for a second show cause notice to be served on an accused government servant yet the Establishment Division, in consultation with the Ministry of Law, has accepted the view that a second show cause notice is a constitutional requirement and that in all future proceedings under these Rules, a second show cause notice should be given to pencils against whom any major penalty is proposed to be awarded. This Office Memorandum, it is found, was issued on 8.8.71 i.e. about 16 days after the impugned order of the respondent, was passed compulsorily retiring the petitioner from service. As to compulsory retirement, it is one of the four major punishments as defined in rule 4 of the Rules of 1976 If this is the view of the government regarding a second show cause notice in the case of a major' punishment the learned Asstt. Attorney General should not have taken a different stand in this case. 

 7. Mr. Shafiuddin has next contended that the provision of Article 135(2) of the Constitution is not attracted by the order for compulsory retirement; it is applicable only in the cases' of dismissal or removal from service or reduction in rank. It is true that this Article does not speak of compulsory retirement from service. But if a person is compulsorily retired from service by way of punishment its effect is same, as that of removal or dismissal from service and in that case it amounts to removal or dismissal. The Indian Supreme Court in a case reported in A.I.R. 1967, SC-1264 held that when an order for compulsory retirement contains express words from which the meaning of Article 311 of the Indian Constitution. This Article corresponds to Article 135 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. In another case, (P.L.D. 1958, S.C. Ind.) 217, the Indian Supreme Court Held that an order of 'reversion' of a government servant by way of penalty amounted to his reduction in rank within the meaning of the same Article, 311, of the Indian Constitution. The Supreme Court of Pakistan held in the case of Golam Sarkar Vs. Pakistan PLD 1962, S.C. 142 that the termination of service of a railway employee amounted to his dismissal from service since it was resorted to by way of punishment. In the case of Md. Ismail Hussain, (1975) 27 DLR 354 a Division Bench of this Court to which one of us was a party held that the reversion of a temporary Circle Officer (Revenue) made mala fide amounted to reduction in rank and-that the order having been made in violation of the provision of Article 135(2) of the Constitution it was void and inoperative. In the instant case the petitioner was compulsorily retired as a measure of major punishment within the meaning of rule 4(5) of the Rules of 1976 and as such it amounted to his removal from service. He was, therefore, entitled to have opportunity to show case why the proposed punishment would not be awarded him. 

 8. Lastly, Mr. Shafiuddin has questioned the maintainability of the application under Article 102 of the Constitution contending that rule 22 of the Rules of 1976 provides for a review against any order of punishment made by the President. In this case, he has submitted, the impugned order having been made by the President the petitioner could have filed an application for review. Article 102 of the Constitution provides that the High Court Division may entertain an application under this Article filed by an aggrieved person if it is satisfied that there is no other equally efficacious remedy provided by law. Mr. Sirajul Hoque has contended that, the remedy by way of review is not equally efficacious and that even where an alternative remedy is available an application under this Article- may lie if the High Court Division is satisfied that the alternative remedy is not available without loss of time and money. Again, the question of alternative remedy, he has argued further, will be of no avail if the impugned order is ex-facie illegal or void being violative of any provision of the Constitution. We find that an alternative remedy was available to the petitioner by way of an application for review which was equally efficacious. There is no substance in the contention of Mr. Sirajul Huq that the remedy by way of review is not efficacious. But we think that an application under Article 102 of the Constitution lies, even where an alternative remedy is available, if the impugned order is ex facie void for want of jurisdiction or is violative of any provision of the Constitution. Violation of any provision of the Constitution is altogether different from violation of any provision of law or rules, such as Service Rules, as referred to in this case. The impugned order having contravened a provision of the Constitution, the application under Article 102 of is quite maintainable.
